findings.blocking_reason: The timing side-channel is on Base64-encoded SHA-512 hash comparison (not plaintext), making practical exploitability near-zero, and the federated-path concern is in test code without a demonstrated production exploit path.
findings.body:
This PR introduces federation support for recovery codes, creating two distinct validation paths that both use non-constant-time String.equals, forming a systemic timing side-channel across the entire recovery code validation surface.

Path 1 (Federated): UserStorageProvider.isValid() handles recovery codes for federated users. The test provider BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage — the de facto reference implementation that third-party user storage providers will copy — uses String.equals on PLAINTEXT recovery codes at line 340 (`key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse())`).

Path 2 (Local): RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.isValid() (line 99-119) calls RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.verifyRecoveryCodeInput() (line 40-43), which uses String.equals on Base64-encoded SHA-512 hash strings (`hashedInputBackupCode.equals(hashedSavedRecoveryCode)`). While hashing provides some mitigation, String.equals short-circuits on the first differing Base64 character, leaking information about the hash prefix and, by extension, the plaintext recovery code.

The PR does not provide a constant-time comparison utility for user storage providers. An individual reviewer might dismiss F-002 as 'test code only,' but the compound view reveals that (1) the same non-constant-time pattern exists in the production utility verifyRecoveryCodeInput, (2) the PR's federation design makes the test provider the reference implementation that third-party developers will replicate, and (3) no constant-time enforcement exists anywhere in the expanded validation surface. This is a systemic control gap: the PR expands the recovery code validation surface without enforcing constant-time comparison in either path.
findings.evidence:
RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.java line 42: `hashedInputBackupCode.equals(hashedSavedRecoveryCode)` — String.equals on Base64-encoded hash in production utility.
BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.java line 340: `generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse()))` — String.equals on plaintext in reference federation provider.
RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.java line 109: calls `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.verifyRecoveryCodeInput(rawInput, nextRecoveryCode)` — local path routes through non-constant-time utility.
RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator.java line 71-72: `authenticatedUser.credentialManager().isValid(...)` — routes to either federated (UserStorageProvider.isValid) or local (RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.isValid) path.
No MessageDigest.isEqual or Arrays.constantTimeEquals call found anywhere in the recovery code validation surface.
findings.suggestion:
1) In RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.verifyRecoveryCodeInput, decode both Base64 strings back to byte arrays and use MessageDigest.isEqual(byte[], byte[]) for constant-time comparison, as was done before this PR replaced it with String.equals.
2) Add a constant-time comparison utility method (e.g., RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.constantTimeEquals) and document in the UserStorageProvider SPI that implementations MUST use it instead of String.equals when validating recovery codes.
3) Update BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid to demonstrate the correct constant-time pattern for federated providers, since it serves as the reference implementation.
4) Add a test that verifies constant-time behavior (e.g., timing comparison across inputs with common prefixes).
findings.title: Systemic non-constant-time recovery code comparison across federated and local storage validation paths

findings.blocking_reason: This is a missing defensive error-handling pattern for an edge case (read-only federated users with exhausted recovery codes) in new code, not a regression, security vulnerability, data loss, or broken contract.
findings.body:
When a user exhausts all recovery codes (allCodesUsed() returns true), the authenticator calls authenticatedUser.addRequiredAction(CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES) directly on the UserModel (L90-92). For users backed by read-only federated user storage providers — the exact scenario this PR enables — ReadOnlyUserModelDelegate.addRequiredAction() throws ReadOnlyException (confirmed at L94-96 of ReadOnlyUserModelDelegate.java). There is no try/catch around this call, so the exception propagates uncaught, causing the authentication flow to fail with a server error instead of gracefully prompting the user to reconfigure recovery codes.

This is inconsistent with the PR's own CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential() (L115-131), which implements a try/fallback pattern: it attempts user.credentialManager().updateCredential() first (for federated providers), then falls back to local credential creation if that returns false. The authenticator's 'codes used up' path should follow the same defensive pattern.

The correct fallback for read-only users is to add the required action to the authentication session instead of the user model: AuthenticationSessionModel.addRequiredAction(RequiredAction) (confirmed at L98 of AuthenticationSessionModel.java) persists the required action for the current auth flow without modifying the user store. The target file already has access to the authentication session via context.getAuthenticationSession().
findings.evidence: RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator.java L90-92: `authenticatedUser.addRequiredAction(UserModel.RequiredAction.CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES)` — no try/catch. ReadOnlyUserModelDelegate.java L94-96: `public void addRequiredAction(RequiredAction action) { throw readOnlyException("required action " + action); }`. AuthenticationSessionModel.java L98: `void addRequiredAction(UserModel.RequiredAction action);` — exists as fallback. CredentialHelper.java L115-131: PR's own createRecoveryCodesCredential() tries federated updateCredential() first, falls back to local createCredential() — same defensive pattern not applied here. Target file is NEW (git log shows `new file mode 100644` for commit ce2dcc537b).
findings.title: Uncaught ReadOnlyException when recovery codes exhausted for federated (read-only) users

findings.blocking_reason: This is a test-only fixture with no production impact; the issues are code quality and schema consistency concerns that don't break the build or affect production behavior.
findings.body:
`getCredentials()` deserializes `myUser.recoveryCodes.getCredentialData()` with raw `List.class` and feeds the result into `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues(List<String> originalGeneratedCodes, long, String)`. This is a contract mismatch on two axes:

1. **Schema divergence.** `updateCredential()` (line 197) stores `input.getChallengeResponse()` — a JSON-serialized `List<String>` of *raw* generated codes — as `credentialData`. Production `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.createCredential()` stores a `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialData` JSON (hash iterations, algorithm, remaining/total counts) in `credentialData` and the *hashed* codes in `secretData` (see `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues`, lines 70-74). The test fixture therefore persists a different `credentialData` schema than production, and never persists `secretData` at all.
2. **Re-hashing side effect.** `createFromValues()` calls `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode()` on each element (line 67). Passing already-stored raw codes through it re-hashes them and synthesizes a fresh `RecoveryAuthnCodesSecretData`. The returned `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel` is thus *not* a faithful representation of what the federated storage persisted — any SPI implementer copying this fixture as a template will build a provider whose `getCredentials()` returns reconstructed, re-hashed models rather than the stored credential.

Because this PR's stated goal is to enable federated user-storage providers for recovery codes, this fixture is now the de-facto reference implementation for downstream SPI authors. The schema divergence and re-hashing behavior are precedent-setting and worth fixing even though the fixture is test-only.

The `List.class` raw deserialization itself (vs. a parameterized `TypeReference<List<String>>`) is the proximate pattern-hygiene defect: it triggers unchecked-conversion warnings, loses the element-type information that `createFromValues`'s signature promises, and masks any future schema drift (e.g., if a provider stores `List<Integer>` codes, this compiles and silently misbehaves at runtime).
findings.dimension_name: BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage contract fidelity and pattern hygiene
findings.evidence:
Step 1: `updateCredential()` (line 193-201) executes `recoveryCodesModel.setCredentialData(input.getChallengeResponse())` — storing a JSON `List<String>` of raw codes as `credentialData`, with no `secretData` set.
Step 2: `getCredentials()` (line 237-241) calls `JsonSerialization.readValue(myUser.recoveryCodes.getCredentialData(), List.class)` and passes the raw `List` to `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues(List<String>, long, String)`.
Step 3: `createFromValues` (server-spi/.../RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.java:58-85) invokes `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode(originalGeneratedCodes.get(i))` on each element, rebuilding `RecoveryAuthnCodesSecretData` with hashed codes and `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialData` with metadata — a schema entirely different from the `List<String>` JSON the fixture stored.
Step 4: Contrast with production `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider` (services/.../RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.java:71), which deserializes `credentialData` as `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialData.class` and uses `createFromCredentialModel()`. The fixture's `List.class` path therefore both mis-types the deserialization and diverges from the production `credentialData` schema.
findings.suggestion:
Deserialize with a parameterized type reference and persist the credential in the production schema so `getCredentials()` can use `createFromCredentialModel()` instead of re-running `createFromValues()`:

```java
// in updateCredential(), store the full model produced by createFromValues:
RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel recoveryCodesModel =
    RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues(
        JsonSerialization.readValue(input.getChallengeResponse(), new TypeReference<List<String>>(){}),
        Time.currentTimeMillis(),
        input.getUserLabel());
users.get(translateUserName(user.getUsername())).recoveryCodes = recoveryCodesModel;
```

Then in `getCredentials()`, return the stored model directly via `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromCredentialModel(myUser.recoveryCodes)` (mirroring `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider` line 71-72). If keeping the current simplified storage shape is intentional for backwards-compat testing, at minimum swap `List.class` for `new TypeReference<List<String>>(){}` and document why the fixture deliberately diverges from the production schema.
findings.title: Raw List.class deserialization violates RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModelcreateFromValues contract and diverges from production credentialData schema

findings.blocking_reason: Code hygiene suggestion in a test fixture with no current correctness or security impact; not reachable as a production defect.
findings.body:
In `isValid()`, the recovery-codes branch declares the raw local `List generatedKeys;` (line 332) and verifies a submitted code via `generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse()))` (line 340). Two hygiene defects:

1. **Raw `List` type.** `generatedKeys` is declared without type parameters, so `key` is `Object`. This compiles only because `JsonSerialization.readValue(..., List.class)` returns raw `List`. It emits unchecked-conversion warnings and silently permits any element type. If a future fixture variant ever persists codes as JSON numbers (or Jackson is configured to coerce), the `key.equals(String)` check would return `false` for every element and every recovery-code login would fail — with no compile-time signal.
2. **Asymmetric equality.** `key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse())` invokes `Object.equals(String)`. For `Object.equals`, the left operand's class owns the equality logic; if `key` is not a `String`, `Object.equals` returns `false` regardless of content. The idiomatic, symmetric form is `input.getChallengeResponse().equals(key)` (or `generatedKeys.contains(input.getChallengeResponse())`), which ensures `String.equals` logic is used. This is the same class of latent bug as the classic `"foo".equals(maybeNull)` ordering rule.

Neither defect breaks the current test path because Jackson deserializes the stored JSON array as `List<String>` at runtime, but both are precedent-setting patterns for SPI implementers reading this fixture as a reference for federated recovery-code validation.
findings.dimension_name: BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage contract fidelity and pattern hygiene
findings.evidence:
Step 1: `isValid()` recovery branch (line 332) declares `List generatedKeys;` — raw type, no type parameters.
Step 2: Line 334 assigns `JsonSerialization.readValue(storedRecoveryKeys.getCredentialData(), List.class)` to it — `readValue(..., List.class)` returns raw `List`, emitting an unchecked-conversion warning.
Step 3: Line 340 calls `generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse()))`. `key` is `Object`; `input.getChallengeResponse()` is `String` (see `UserCredentialModel.getChallengeResponse()` at server-spi/.../UserCredentialModel.java:153). `Object.equals(String)` dispatches to `Object.equals` unless `key` is a `String` at runtime.
Step 4: If Jackson ever materializes a non-String element (e.g., numeric coercion, schema drift), `key.equals(String)` returns `false` for every element and the recovery-code login silently fails — no compile error.
findings.title: Raw List local variable and asymmetric Object.equals(String) comparison in isValid() recovery-codes verification

findings.body:
The two sibling test providers in the same package — `FailableHardcodedStorageProvider` (lines 139, 197) and `HardcodedRoleStorageProvider` (lines 162, 192) — consistently declare `List<String>` for attribute-value typing. This fixture is the first in the package to use raw `List.class` for Jackson deserialization (lines 238 and 334). Keycloak's own `JsonSerialization` supports `TypeReference` for parameterized collection deserialization, and production code (e.g., `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider` line 71) uses typed `*.class` targets rather than `List.class`. Aligning the fixture with the parameterized `List<String>` pattern used by its siblings would eliminate the warnings and match the package's prevailing convention.
